drivers.evidence: Two past weeks at $4.56: 2026-09-28 (x0.94) and 2026-10-05 (x0.57). Noise-adjusted average: x0.91. This week has no promotion, so no offset. Use x0.91, shrunk to -9% for uncertainty.

adjustment.analysis: The target week has no events and a price increase to $4.56 (+5.1% vs regular $4.34). Recent weeks show a clear price sensitivity: at $4.56, sales dropped to 119 units (2026-10-05), 195 (2026-09-28), and 180 (2026-09-07) — all below baseline. The 2026-09-28 week (also $4.56) sold at 195 units (vs baseline 207.6), a 6% drop. With no promotion or event, and a price increase, demand is expected to fall. The noise-adjusted effect of past price hikes (at $4.56) is x0.91 (median of two weeks). No promotion is planned, so no uplift. The classical model’s x1.00 is too high. Shrink toward 1.0 due to limited data and price-only effect.

brief:
PRODUCT: Whole Milk 1 gal | category Dairy | Store #12 (Austin, TX)
TARGET WEEK: 2026-11-16 to 2026-11-22 (6 weeks after the last week with sales data)

KNOWN PLAN FOR THE TARGET WEEK:
  events: none
  shelf price: 4.56 (+5.1% vs regular price 4.34)

STATISTICAL BASELINE (exponential smoothing of recent sales; it ignores events, promotions and prices):
  median 207.6 | 5%-95%: 133.3 - 290.5 | 10%-90%: 156.2 - 281.3

In the evidence below, 'vs baseline' = actual units / what this same baseline predicted for that week.
It is the multiplier that would have been right, so it maps directly onto median_multiplier.
This product's ordinary weeks already swing about +/-22% around the baseline, so a past effect smaller than that, seen only a few times, is mostly noise. The
'noise-adjusted estimate' is the effect shrunk toward x1.0 for that noise and the number of sightings.
